claims.text: A random elemental distribution in high-entropy nanoalloys produces severe lattice distortion.
Lattice distortion increases the energy barriers for atomic diffusion and produces sluggish diffusion.
Sluggish diffusion raises the kinetic barrier to grain-boundary migration and thereby inhibits grain growth.
Sluggish diffusion raises the kinetic barrier to precipitation and thereby preserves chemical homogeneity.
Diffusion barriers associated with lattice distortion govern the high-temperature structural and chemical stability of high-entropy nanoalloys.
A magnetron-sputtered refractory high-entropy alloy film can have an initial grain size of approximately 20–30 nm.
The proposed initial refractory high-entropy alloy has a homogeneous elemental distribution.
The high-entropy nanoalloy should be annealed at about 1173 K for a fixed duration.
The annealing comparison should use an inert atmosphere with controlled ramp rates and dwell times.
A conventional or lower-configurational-entropy alloy with similar initial grain size should be processed and annealed identically as the control.
The nanocrystalline initial state has a high density of grain boundaries.
The chemically disordered state produces local lattice distortions.
A high-entropy nanoalloy should exhibit minimal grain growth after annealing near 1173 K.
The high-entropy nanoalloy should exhibit less grain growth than the conventional or lower-entropy control.
The high-entropy nanoalloy should show negligible secondary-phase formation or segregation after annealing.
The conventional control will undergo greater grain coarsening and chemical inhomogeneity because it has faster diffusion.
The predicted stabilization can persist through annealing at approximately 1173 K.
At more extreme temperatures, evaporation or other high-temperature reactions may override the proposed stabilization mechanism.
The magnitude of grain-growth inhibition, the breakdown temperature, and composition-specific diffusion barriers are uncertain.
Comparable or greater grain coarsening or secondary-phase formation in the high-entropy alloy relative to the control would falsify the proposed enhanced-stability mechanism.
